name: Incident reporting and investigation
summary: Workers report injuries, near misses, equipment damage and spills to their supervisor, who makes the area safe and writes the incident report before the end of shift; the first aid attendant treats injuries and drives serious cases an hour to hospital. A safety coordinator classifies each report, files WSIB and ministry notices when due, and leads formal investigations of serious or high-potential events with a committee worker member, after which managers approve corrective actions and a safety alert goes out. A critical injury requires immediate notice to the ministry, an untouched scene and a written report within 48 hours. Investigations stall on 14-on/14-off rotations, on managers' review queues, and on corrective actions that wait for parts or shutdowns.

baseline.org_archetype: A single-mine Canadian gold producer running a 500-650 tpd underground mine and its own mill near Wawa in northern Ontario, with 12-hour shifts on 14-on/14-off rotations and a camp.
baseline.notes: About 380 people on the site roster including contractors; the mine encourages near-miss reporting.

unit_of_work: one incident (injury, near miss, equipment damage or spill)
trigger: A worker or supervisor reports an incident.
end_state: The incident is classified, required notices are filed, causes are recorded and the corrective actions are verified as done.

volume.seasonality: Slightly higher in winter (slips on surface, cold-weather equipment failures) and after crew changes; no strong pattern.

evidence.note: Kept from the organisation file: tens of incidents and near misses a month for a site roster of about 380 people.
Eight supervisors share first response, reports, supervisor reviews and corrective actions.
First aid response and hospital trips.
Three coordinators on rotation; incident triage, notices, investigations and verification take about half of their combined time.
Reviews investigations, critical injury notices and orders.
Spill reports.
Signs off serious investigations.

systems.name: Incident, inspection and training records system
Leaky feeder radio and surface radio network
Shared drives and document library (procedures, permits, drawings)
Maintenance management system (ERP maintenance module or standalone)
Environmental monitoring data workbooks and lab certificates

steps.name: Take the report and make the area safe
steps.description: A worker reports an injury, near miss, equipment damage or spill to the shift supervisor by radio or in person. The supervisor goes to the scene, stops work nearby, barricades or isolates the hazard, and decides whether first aid or the emergency response is needed.

control.basis: Mine health and safety program: stop work and isolate the hazard after an incident (OHSA duty of the supervisor to protect workers)

next.condition: near miss, damage or spill with no injury

evidence.note: Share of incidents with an injury is the author's estimate; near misses and property damage usually outnumber injuries at mines that encourage reporting.

steps.name: Give first aid and assess the injury
steps.description: The industrial first aid attendant, called by radio, reaches the worker, treats the injury, records the treatment in the first aid log and decides whether the worker can return to work, needs a doctor, or is seriously hurt.

control.basis: Ontario Regulation 1101 (first aid requirements) under the Workplace Safety and Insurance Act: first aid treatment recorded

next.condition: first aid only, back to work

evidence.note: Shares are the author's estimate; the regulation was not opened.

steps.name: Take the injured worker to hospital
steps.description: The first aid attendant drives the worker in the site emergency vehicle to the hospital in Wawa, about an hour away, hands over to the emergency department and returns. If the worker is underground the trip starts with the cage or a ramp vehicle.

evidence.note: The technical report places the complex near Wawa with Sault Ste. Marie about four hours away; drive time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Write the incident report
steps.description: Before the end of shift the supervisor writes the incident report in the incident system, or on the paper form when the system is not reachable underground: what happened, who was involved, the immediate cause and what was done to make the area safe.

error.defect_description: Report is vague on the sequence of events or leaves out contributing conditions.

control.basis: Company incident reporting standard: every incident reported before the end of shift

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice at Ontario mines.

steps.name: Evacuate the critically injured worker
steps.description: The first aid attendant and mine rescue members stabilize the worker, bring them to surface by cage or ramp and hand over to the ambulance or air ambulance at the site landing area.

evidence.note: The technical report mentions an emergency landing site for the provincial air ambulance; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Notify the ministry, committee and union and preserve the scene
steps.description: The HSE manager phones the ministry's health and safety contact centre and tells the joint health and safety committee, has security guard the scene so nothing is moved, and informs the general manager and the chief operating officer.

control.basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 51: immediate notice of a critical injury or death and the scene left undisturbed until released by an inspector

evidence.note: Immediate notice, scene preservation and recipients from the ministry page; minutes are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Inspector investigates at the scene
steps.description: A mining inspector travels to site, examines the scene, interviews witnesses and the supervisor, and releases the scene; the inspector may write orders on the spot. The wait covers the drive from the district office and the investigation days.

next.condition: no orders or orders complied with on the spot
orders issued that need a written compliance plan

evidence.note: Inspector attendance after critical injuries is normal ministry practice; times and the share with orders are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Send the 48-hour written report
steps.description: The safety coordinator writes the formal report to the ministry with the circumstances, the injured worker's details, witnesses and the steps taken, has the HSE manager sign it and sends it within 48 hours.

control.basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 51(1) and O. Reg. 420/21: written report to a Director within 48 hours of a critical injury or death

evidence.note: 48-hour deadline from the ministry page; drafting time is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Classify the incident and decide the level of review
steps.description: The next day on site the safety coordinator reads the report in the incident system, phones the supervisor for missing facts, classifies the incident (first aid, medical aid, lost time, near miss, damage, spill) and its potential severity, and decides whether a supervisor review is enough or a formal investigation is needed. They also check whether a WSIB report, a two-day mine notice or a spill report is due.

next.condition: medical attention or lost time: WSIB and notices due
high potential or lost time: formal investigation

evidence.note: Triage practice and shares are the author's estimate; reporting rules from the ministry and WSIB pages.

steps.name: File the WSIB Form 7 and written notices
steps.description: The safety coordinator, with the site HR coordinator, completes the WSIB Form 7 online within three business days and gives the four-day written notice to the joint health and safety committee; for a reportable mine accident the two-day notice also goes to the ministry. Modified work is arranged with the supervisor.

error.defect_description: Form filed late or with the wrong date of injury.

control.basis: Workplace Safety and Insurance Act: Form 7 within three business days; OHSA s. 52 and Regulation 854: written notice within four days (two days for listed mine accidents)

evidence.note: Deadlines from the WSIB and ministry pages; the WSIB page is the 2026 version and the three-day rule was the author's understanding of 2019-2022 practice too.

steps.name: Supervisor reviews the cause and fixes the hazard
steps.description: For a low-potential incident the supervisor talks to the people involved, records the cause and a simple corrective action in the incident system (fix a guard, re-scale, replace a hose, re-instruct a worker), and does it on the next shift where possible.

error.defect_description: Cause recorded as 'worker error' without the underlying condition.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice.

steps.name: Report the spill and arrange clean-up
steps.description: The environmental coordinator decides whether the spill (diesel, hydraulic oil, process solution) must be reported to the provincial Spills Action Centre, phones it in if so, and arranges clean-up and soil sampling with the mill or surface crew.

control.basis: Ontario Environmental Protection Act, Part X: report spills of pollutants to the ministry Spills Action Centre

evidence.note: Spill reporting duty under the Environmental Protection Act is well known; the act was not opened, and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Set up the investigation team
steps.description: The safety coordinator names the investigation team (the area supervisor, a joint committee worker member and a technical person such as a mechanic or engineer), books a time that fits the crews' rotation, and gathers photos, equipment records and training records.

evidence.note: Joint committee worker participation in investigations is normal Ontario practice; the wait reflects people being on their days off on a 14/14 rotation.

steps.name: Inspect the scene and interview witnesses
steps.description: The team visits the scene, takes measurements and photos, and interviews the people involved and witnesses one at a time, writing statements on the investigation form.

evidence.note: Three-person team for two to ten hours is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Analyse causes and draft the investigation report
steps.description: The safety coordinator works through the sequence of events with a root-cause method (five whys or a causal tree), lists immediate and underlying causes, and proposes corrective actions with owners and dates in the incident system.

error.defect_description: Corrective actions address the symptom, or owners and dates are vague.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Review the report and agree corrective actions
steps.description: The HSE manager and the superintendent of the department involved read the draft, challenge weak causes, and agree corrective actions, owners and due dates.

control.basis: Company incident investigation standard: HSE manager approves formal investigations

next.condition: lost time, critical or high potential: general manager review

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: General manager signs off the investigation
steps.description: The general manager reads the serious investigations, confirms the corrective actions and resources, and forwards the report to the chief operating officer for the board's health and safety committee.

control.basis: Company governance: general manager sign-off of serious incident investigations and board reporting

evidence.note: Author's estimate of governance at a listed single-mine producer.

steps.name: Issue a safety alert
steps.description: The safety coordinator writes a one-page safety alert with what happened, why, and what changes, posts it on the boards and sends it to supervisors and the trainers for line-up talks and refresher training.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Carry out the corrective actions
steps.description: The department supervisor or the planner carries out the agreed actions: a procedure change, a guard or engineering fix through a maintenance work order, retraining, or a change to the line-up. Larger actions wait for parts or the next shutdown.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; corrective actions commonly run for weeks.

steps.name: Present the findings to the joint health and safety committee
steps.description: At its monthly meeting the joint health and safety committee reviews the investigation and the safety alert, and its worker members can ask for further actions. This runs while the actions are being carried out.

control.basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act s. 9: the joint health and safety committee receives information on incidents and makes recommendations

evidence.note: Committee role under OHSA s. 9 is well known; the act was not opened.

steps.name: Verify the actions and close the incident
steps.description: The safety coordinator checks each action in the field or against evidence (a closed work order, a signed training record), closes the incident in the system, or reopens actions that did not fix the hazard.

next.condition: action not done or not effective

evidence.note: Author's estimate; coordinators verify open actions in a weekly or rotation-end sweep, so closure waits one to two weeks after the work is done.

steps.name: Answer the inspector's orders
steps.description: The HSE manager writes the compliance plan for each order (what will be done and by when), gets the general manager's agreement, and sends the notice of compliance to the ministry when the work is done.

control.basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act: compliance with inspector's orders and notice of compliance

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the act was not opened.

exceptions.name: Critical injury
exceptions.description: Immediate phone notice to the ministry, committee and union, the scene held for the inspector, a 48-hour written report and a full investigation; orders may follow.

exceptions.name: Lost-time or medical-aid injury
exceptions.description: WSIB Form 7 within three business days and the four-day written notice, then a supervisor review or formal investigation.

exceptions.name: Corrective action not effective
exceptions.description: The coordinator finds the action not done or not working and sends it back.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from report to incident closed
benchmarks.population: Incidents at an Ontario underground mine with a 14/14 rotation

evidence.note: Supervisor-level reviews close in two to four weeks once the action is verified; formal investigations with engineered fixes run one to three months.

benchmarks.unit: business days after learning of the injury

pain_points.description: Investigation teams wait for people to come back on rotation, so a formal investigation can lose one or two weeks before the scene interviews.

evidence.note: 14/14 rotation from the organisation file; effect is the author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Supervisors write reports at the end of a 12-hour shift; vague reports come back from triage.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Corrective actions that need parts, engineering or a shutdown stay open for weeks and need repeated chasing.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

sources.title: Reporting workplace incidents and illnesses
sources.publisher: Ontario Ministry of Labour, Training and Skills Development (archived copy in the Library and Archives Canada web archive)
sources.supports: Fatality or critical injury: notify the ministry, the joint health and safety committee or representative, and the union immediately; do not disturb the scene except to save life, relieve suffering, keep essential services or prevent property damage, or with an inspector's permission; written report to the ministry within 48 hours. At a mine or mining plant, written notice within two days of an accident, explosion, fire, inrush of water, cave-in or certain equipment failures even if no one is hurt. Written notice within four days to the committee and union when a worker is disabled from work or needs medical attention because of an accident. Copies kept three years. Page published 29 August 2018, updated 7 July 2022; capture of 4 January 2023.

sources.title: Report an injury or illness (businesses)
sources.supports: Employers report to the WSIB on Form 7 within three business days of learning of an injury that needs health care beyond first aid, causes absence, lost earnings or modified work at less than regular pay, or modified work at regular pay for more than seven days; first-aid-only injuries are not reported; penalties and prosecution for late or missing reports. Page updated 2 September 2026.

sources.title: Technical Report for the Eagle River Gold Mining Complex, Ontario, Canada (NI 43-101)
sources.publisher: SRK Consulting (Canada) Inc. for Wesdome Gold Mines Ltd.
sources.supports: Section 20.4: monitoring under the ECAs, the PTTW and the MDMER covers effluent flow and quality during discharge, effluent toxicity tests, groundwater and receiving water; treated effluent from the Mill polishing pond to Miron Creek is discharged at controlled rates through most of the year, with little or none in February-March and August-September; the Eagle River Mine settling ponds discharge continuously to Lake C7; the Mishi pit ponds discharged to Macassa Creek as needed, mainly in spring and fall, during pit operations; 2020 annual reports met MDMER and ECA limits, with copper, free cyanide and un-ionized ammonia above ECA objectives at the Mill and one monthly dissolved aluminum exceedance at Mishi; EEM biological studies every three years. Section 11.2: water and effluent analyses by Testmark Laboratories (Thunder Bay, ISO 17025 accredited through CALA) and toxicity tests by Nautilus Environmental (Oakville). Section 17: cyanide in reclaim pond water treated with hydrogen peroxide. Table 20-1: Mill ECA peak flow 4,750 m3/day. Section 18 lists a warehouse among site buildings.

assumptions: Branch shares (30% injuries, 6% needing WSIB reporting, 25% formal investigations, 0.3% critical) are the author's estimates; no incident statistics for the site were opened.
The WSIB step is reached from triage with its overall share rather than only from the injury path, because the simulator does not carry memory of earlier branches.

The organisation file lists only mine-shift-control and mnt-breakdown-repair as triggers; incidents also come from the mill and from contractors, so mill-grind-leach and site-contractors were added as triggers. Corrective actions produce maintenance work requests and spills produce reports to the ministry of the environment.
The simulated median of about 16 days is below the 21-day estimate because most incidents take the supervisor-review path; formal investigations drive the 45-day 90th percentile.
The site emergency vehicle is not in the organisation file and was added as a resource.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's rates: base wage times 1.30 for office and staff roles and 1.35 for hourly site roles.

Organisation file corrected on 2026-11-24 to match this workflow's sources: ids were renamed (mill-elution-refining to mill-gold-room-refining, loaded_carbon to gold_concentrate, tailings_slurry to filtered_tailings, elution-circuit to refinery), and roles and resources this workflow added are now in the organisation file. Notes above that describe a mismatch refer to the file before the correction.
